rv.q: It's impossible not to be carried away by the brio of the whole thing...

But this absolutely would not work without McArdle, whose combination of louche intellectualism, ebullient physicality and startling inner seriousness is just perfect – he plays the complicated role like some sort of esoteric string instrument.
In Stoppard’s tricksy hall of mirrors vision, thrillingly returned to the stage at the Old Vic by Max Webster, they are addictively bewildering.
This super-smart 1982 comedy represents Stoppard’s own wrestle with the same conundrum.
The longer it goes on, the more this production finds a plangent tone where the witty, the wise and the wounded are forever colliding.

Now, at the Old Vic, we have James McArdle and Bel Powley. The play is starting to show its age — with Henry calling Annie a 'silly cow' and telling her to 'shut up and listen'. And Stoppard's lofty preoccupation with Shakespeare, and what makes truly great literature, can feel out of touch.

This is Stoppard at his tricksy best but simultaneously at his most sincere, it seems, because at this drama’s heart is a timeless study of passion and art that 40 years on remains – rather like the insides of a well-made Swiss watch – exquisitely intact.
But while Max Webster’s production delivers consummate style (not least the choreographed manoeuvres of the scene-shifting stage-hands), its emotional substance is more uneven.
On it goes, slick but arid and when it ends it’s a challenge to know what we’re meant to take away from it.
But it is also airless and bloodless, its ingenious construction and innate snobbery a barrier to genuine emotional engagement.

The Real Thing offers a less deeply felt, more snobbish perspective on the ills of the left – and there’s something resolutely unfashionable about its spectacle of adulterous middle-class couples being beastly to each other in beige living rooms.
Revisited, The Real Thing feels fake.
Webster’s production emphasises the constant intermingling of life and performance through Peter McKintosh’s set, Richard Howell’s lighting and Chi-San Howard’s movement.
The Real Thing is very much ado about something and moves through, as it were, The French Lieutenant’s Woman via Les Liaisons Dangereuses to Pinter’s Betrayal.

All in all, then, this is a sophisticated and enjoyable revival of a play that still, beneath its beautiful veneer of humour, has the heft to raise troubling and endlessly fascinating questions about the state of the human heart and how we describe it.
This is Stoppard with both brains and heart, its jokes showered like confetti.
This dazzlingly funny play is not revived as frequently as it deserves to be.
The Real Thing is itself finely crafted, clever and funny; it holds our attention but doesn’t involve our emotions.
If that sounds hard work and just a bit intellectually incestuous, it is, but not immediately.
Stoppard's wit, wisdom, verbal dexterity and playmaking, still make for revelatory and thrilling theatre.
This slick revival of his 1982 comedy is a reminder of why we care.
Sometimes it’s fun to simply watch a master expertly place one word before the next in an order that frequently takes your breath away.

cn.t: Stoppard's witty, cerebral play about love and art dazzles with verbal brilliance but divides critics on emotional depth. McArdle's performance as the mansplaining playwright Henry wins praise, though some find the work hollow and dated.
